OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$ and all polynomials $P$ of degree $n$ with coefficients $\pm 1$,\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert > (1+c)\sqrt{n}?\]
#1150: [Ha74,4.31][Va99,2.36]
analysis | 
polynomials
In other words, does there exist an 'ultraflat' polynomial with coefficients $\pm 1$. The answer is yes if the coefficients can take any values on the unit circle (see [230]).
The lower bound\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert\geq \sqrt{n}\]is trivial from Parseval's theorem.
A weaker 'flatness' question is the subject of [228].

 I would like to answer the question concerning the correct reference for Erdős Problem \#1150. It is the following (I mentioned in one of my papers):
P. Erdős, Extremal problems on polynomials, Approximation Theory II, 1976, 347-355.
Therein, Erdős wrote (page 354): "Some of these questions may not be 'serious' Mathematics, but I am sure the following final problem, considered by D. J. Newman and myself for a long time, is both difficult and interesting."
I am taking this opportunity to emphasize that the constant $c_p$ is defined as the largest possible constant $c$ such that for any symmetric non empty open set $E$ 
$$\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}}\frac{\int_E |P(z)|^p dz}{\int |P(z)|^p dz}>c.$$
the supremum is taking over all idempotent (Bourgain–Newman) polynomials (https://arxiv.org/pdf/0707.3023, Definition 2 (cf. also Theorem 7)). Moreover, the Vitali theorem is proved in my published paper, with an appendix by M. G. Nadkarni: \url{https://pcwww.liv.ac.uk/~karpenk/JournalUDT/vol15/no1/03\%20AbdNad.pdf}. 
The second fundamental result used appears in \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.06439}. A simpler proof of it was posted on arXiv here: arXiv:2210.15480.
Many thanks for all the comments; they will be taken into account in the next version. Further comments, suggestions, questions, or collaboration proposals are very welcome. 
el-Houcein el Abdalaoui.

 I performed a Gemini Deep Research query for related literature and it brought up this paper by el Abdalaoui [El25] which seems to answer this problem in the affirmative by proving that there does not exist an ultraflat polynomial with coefficients $\pm1$.
[El25] cites [Od18], where Odlyzko made progress on this problem via computational methods. Oddly enough, el Abdalaoui also cites problem 22 in [Er57] as the problem they are providing an answer to, but that problem reads like [230]. Maybe someone with more expertise can take a look at this literature and confirm or deny my understanding.

 There are, I believe, multiple serious issues with this paper (I remember discussing with others when it appeared). For example, the final step of the proof on page 9 does not contradict Lemma 5, since the latter is just about the existence of one function with concentration, rather than proving concentration for all functions. I can't recall what the other problems were, but it seemed overall unfixable.

 ChatGPT Pro identifies multiple issues with this preprint. Another cause for concern is that the paper relies heavily on a sequence of the author's preprints dating as far back as 2014, almost all of which remain unpublished. I would assess the claims of this preprint as unconfirmed until the preprint is published (or if there is another source of verification, e.g., by an independent human expert, or with a Lean formalization).
